title: Akal Ustat
hookLine: praise of the Timeless One in many meters

lines: A DRUM, A LULLABY, A CHANT.
A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT IT DOES.
cards: A marching drum. Then a lullaby. Then a fast, tumbling chant, the kind that makes your tongue work.
Then something slow enough to walk to. If a single poem changed its rhythm that often, you'd expect it to change its subject too. This one doesn't.
Every beat, every speed, points at the same One. It sits inside the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs pray parts of it in the morning. Its name is a description of what it does.

teach.b: Akal Ustat: praise of the Timeless One. Akal is the One beyond time, the One that death and change don't reach. Ustat is praise.
The poem moves through many meters, many verse forms, as if every rhythm in the poet's ear had to take a turn.
It opens with a line of shelter, given here in paraphrase: the Timeless Being is my protector; the All-Steel is my protector.
All-Steel, Sarab Loh, is a name for God that sounds like a blade, the strength that doesn't bend. So praise begins by leaning. Before anything grand, it says: I'm held.
Then come the stanzas recited in the Sikh morning prayers, the swayyas called Tav Prasad. A long parade, in paraphrase: I have seen the pure and the holy men, ascetics and yogis.
I have seen mighty kings with elephants and banners, armies stretching away. I have seen pilgrims bathing at sacred places.
And then the turn that comes back again and again: without the love of the Lord, without His grace, all of it counts for nothing.
One stanza ends with a line tradition holds dear, again in paraphrase: I speak the truth, all of you, listen; only those who loved have found the Lord. That's the engine of the poem.
It doesn't mock kings or pilgrims.

teach.h: ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.
teach.b: It walks past them with open eyes and says that the Timeless One is reached by love, not by size.
Praise, in Akal Ustat, isn't flattery. It's a way of putting things back in their right scale: the armies are small, and the One is not.

how: Sikhs recite the Tav Prasad swayyas from Akal Ustat as part of their morning prayers, and stanzas of Akal Ustat are sung as kirtan in gurdwaras.

o: a hymn of thanks for a battle won long ago
a list of the Gurus' names said each morning
praise of the Timeless One, beyond death and change

games.q: inside the name and the poem: tap the pairs.
p: the All-Steel, a name for God

s: Akal Ustat keeps to a single meter throughout
it moves through many meters, all praising the same One.
the Tav Prasad swayyas mock kings and pilgrims
they walk past them and say that without love of the Lord it all counts for nothing.
the poem opens by naming the Timeless as protector
the Timeless Being is my protector; the All-Steel is my protector.

games.q: you have seen holy men, kings with elephants and armies, pilgrims at sacred waters. who, says the poem, has found the Lord?
o: those who bathed at the most holy places.
games.why: the swayyas pass each one by and end: only those who loved have found the Lord.

practice: If you can, let a recording of the Tav Prasad swayyas play, and listen for the rhythm more than the words.
If not, let the parade pass in your mind, the kings, the armies, the pilgrims, and then let the last line arrive: only those who loved. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Akal Ustat. Praise of the Timeless One, in many meters: the poem that walks past kings and pilgrims and says the Lord is found by love. Today's word.

orig.note: akal, the Timeless; ustat, praise. the poem's name says what it does.

carryVoice: Your line: praise of the timeless. Every rhythm in the poem points at one subject. See you tomorrow.
